record.paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
record.original_question: For a suspension of solid particles near a solid wall, what boundary-layer structure forms and how does that boundary layer influence the overall or general macroscopic flow of the suspension?

evidence.quote: boundary layers near a solid wall

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a suspension consisting of a Newtonian fluid carrying a dilute or moderately concentrated set of rigid solid particles, governed at the microscale by the Stokes (or Navier–Stokes) equations in the fluid domain together with no-slip conditions on each particle and on a fixed solid wall. Introduce three characteristic length scales: a typical particle size R, a typical interparticle distance h, and a macroscopic length L with R, h ≪ L. Away from the wall, classical homogenization yields an effective (averaged) constitutive law and an effective macroscopic flow equation for the suspension.

Near the solid wall, however, the periodic or statistical microstructure assumed in the bulk is broken: particles cannot intersect the wall, so a thin transition region of thickness comparable to R or h forms in which the local particle distribution, the local stress, and the local velocity field differ from their bulk homogenized expressions.

Problem. Rigorously characterize this wall boundary layer for a suspension of rigid particles in a viscous fluid. Specifically:
(a) Determine the asymptotic structure (thickness, profile of velocity, local volume fraction, and stress) of the boundary layer that develops between the solid wall and the bulk homogenized suspension as R/L, h/L → 0.
(b) Derive the effective boundary condition (e.g., a slip law, a wall stress relation, or a corrected no-slip condition) that must be imposed on the bulk homogenized flow equations to account for this layer.
(c) Quantify how this boundary layer modifies the macroscopic flow of the suspension (apparent viscosity, apparent slip, drag) compared with the prediction obtained from the bulk homogenized model alone.
artifact.category_tag: Homogenization of suspensions and wall boundary layers
artifact.status_search_result: A rigorous, general derivation of the wall boundary layer for suspensions of rigid particles and the resulting effective wall condition for the homogenized macroscopic flow is not established. While related rough-wall homogenization (Navier-type slip laws) and particle-laden boundary layer reviews exist, a complete characterization for suspension homogenization near a solid wall remains an open question discussed in surveys of homogenization in mechanics.

status_evidence.title: Effective boundary conditions at a rough wall: a high-order homogenization approach
status_evidence.snippet: Homogenization yielding effective Navier-type slip boundary conditions at rough walls, related but distinct from suspensions.
status_evidence.claim: Effective wall conditions via homogenization are an active area; suspension case is more delicate.

status_evidence.title: Homogenized Models of Suspension Dynamics
status_evidence.snippet: Bulk homogenization theory for suspensions; treatment of wall boundary layers remains less developed.
status_evidence.claim: Bulk homogenization of suspensions is well-developed but near-wall corrections are not fully resolved.

status_evidence.title: Particle-Laden Two-Phase Boundary Layer: A Review
status_evidence.snippet: Review surveys experimental and computational work on particle-laden boundary layers, indicating outstanding modeling questions.
status_evidence.claim: Particle-laden boundary layer structure and feedback on macroscopic flow remain modeling challenges.
